text: Most planets spin like slightly tilted tops. Earth leans over by about 23 degrees. Uranus is tipped by about 98 degrees, so it lies almost on its side and rolls around the Sun like a ball rolling along a track.

Nobody saw this happen, so nobody knows for sure why. The most popular idea is that, billions of years ago, something about the size of Earth crashed into young Uranus and knocked it over. Other scientists think several smaller crashes, or the long, slow pull of a moon that no longer exists, might have done the job.

About six months

st.reveal: A year on Uranus lasts about 84 Earth years. For roughly half of that orbit, one pole points towards the Sun, so it has daylight for about 42 years in a row. Then it gets 42 years of darkness.

myth: Uranus has always been known, like the other planets.
The ancients knew five planets besides Earth, all bright enough to see easily. Uranus is so faint that it was recorded as a star until William Herschel noticed in 1781 that it moved.

sec.t:
On 13 March 1781, the musician and [[astronomer|astronomer]] William Herschel was studying stars from his garden in Bath, England. He was using a [[@telescopes-how|telescope]] he had built himself. One "star" looked like a tiny disc instead of a point, and over the next nights it moved.

Herschel first thought it was a [[comet|comet]]. Other astronomers worked out its path and realised it was a planet, the first discovered with a telescope. Herschel wanted to name it after King George III. In the end the name Uranus won, after the Greek god of the sky.

The discovery doubled the size of the known [[solar-system|solar system]] overnight, because Uranus is about twice as far from the Sun as Saturn. The king gave Herschel a yearly salary so that he could give up music and study the sky full time.

{{story:shakespeare}}

Because Uranus is on its side, its [[@seasons-why|seasons]] are extreme. A year there lasts about 84 Earth years. For about half of that, the north pole points roughly towards the Sun and never sees night. For the other half, it sits in darkness while the south pole gets the sunshine.

Picture a child born at Uranus's north pole at the start of its long summer. They would be in their forties before they saw a sunset. Only near the [[equinox|equinoxes]], when the Sun shines on Uranus's middle, does the planet get something like ordinary days and nights, each lasting about 17 hours.

Uranus is about four times as wide as Earth. Astronomers call it an [[@space-weird-hot-ice|ice giant]]. Underneath its clouds is a deep, hot, slushy layer of water, ammonia and methane, much thicker than any ocean on Earth. Methane gas high in its air soaks up red light, giving the planet its pale blue-green colour.

It is also bitterly cold. Uranus has recorded the lowest temperature of any planet's [[atmosphere|atmosphere]], about −224°C. That puzzles scientists, because its near twin, [[@neptune-winds|Neptune]], is even farther from the Sun but gives off much more heat from inside.

Only one spacecraft has ever been to Uranus. [[@voyager|Voyager 2]] flew past in January 1986. In a few hours of close-up work it measured the planet's magnetic field and found ten new moons. Uranus now has more than two dozen known moons. Most are named after characters from the plays of William Shakespeare, such as Miranda, Titania and Oberon, with a couple from a poem by Alexander Pope.

Uranus also has 13 known rings, first detected in 1977. They are thin and dark, very different from Saturn's bright icy ones.

Scientists in the United States have named a mission to [[orbit|orbit]] Uranus as a top priority. If it flies, it would be the first proper look at this tilted world in more than half a century.

text: An airport is a giant sorting machine. It sorts people, bags and planes, and sends each to the right place at the right time. Passengers go one way, through check-in, security and boarding gates. Their bags go another, along hidden conveyor belts. Planes go a third way, along taxiways to the runway.

Behind all this are thousands of workers you rarely see: fuel crews, cleaners, caterers, engineers, [[@jobs-firefighter|firefighters]] and [[@air-traffic|air traffic controllers]]. At big airports such as Atlanta in the United States or Delhi in India, the whole system runs day and night, and a single delayed flight can ripple through dozens of others.

sec.t:
Airports are split into two zones. The "landside" is open to anyone: car parks, drop-off lanes and check-in halls. The "airside" is everything past security, including the departure gates, the aprons where planes park and the runways themselves.

To move from one side to the other you must show a ticket and pass through security screening. On international flights you also visit immigration, where officers check your [[@passports|passport]], and on arrival you may go through [[customs|customs]], where goods you carry can be checked. Every rule is about one question: who and what is allowed near the planes.

sec.h: The secret life of a suitcase

sec.t:
A runway is not just a long road. It is built with thick layers of concrete or asphalt to take the thump of a landing jet weighing hundreds of tonnes. Big airports often have runways 3–4 km long, about as long as 30 to 40 football fields laid end to end.

Each runway is painted with a number from its compass direction. Pilots prefer to take off and land facing into the wind, which gives extra lift at a lower speed. That is why airports in windy places often have runways pointing in different directions, and why the runway in use can change during the day.

sec.h: A city with its own rules
sec.t:
Big airports have their own fire stations, with crews trained to reach any point on a runway within a few minutes. They have power plants, water supplies, hotels and shops. Some are working on cleaner energy. In 2015, [[@kochi|Kochi's]] Cochin International Airport in Kerala began running entirely on [[@solar-panels|solar power]], from fields of panels next to the runway. It is often described as the first airport in the world to do so.

Airports must keep animals away too. Birds sucked into engines are a real danger, so many airports use trained falcons, loud noises or careful grass cutting to keep flocks from settling near the runways. Airports also keep an eye on nearby ponds and rubbish dumps, since both attract birds.

text: Most of the noise of a flying bird comes from air rushing and tumbling off the edges of its wings. [[@owl-eyes|Owls]] have feathers that calm that air down. The front edge of each main wing feather has a row of tiny stiff teeth, like a comb. The back edge is soft and frayed. The surface is covered in velvety fuzz.

Together, these break up big noisy swirls of air into many tiny quiet ones, and soak up the sound of feathers rubbing. Owls also have big wings for their weight, so they can fly slowly and glide often. To a mouse rustling in the grass, an owl arrives with almost no warning. Engineers have copied owl feathers to design quieter fans and trains.

options.t: Fish underwater can't hear the wingbeats anyway
Fish owls only hunt at noon

quiz.reveal: Silence matters most when prey has sharp ears, like a mouse in the grass. A fish under the water's surface can't hear an owl's wings, so fish owls have lost most of these features and fly noisily.

d.try: Wave a stiff piece of cardboard quickly past your ear and listen to the whoosh. Then glue or tape a fringe of cotton wool or soft cloth along one edge and try again. Is it quieter? That soft edge is the owl's trick.
myth: Owls can turn their heads all the way round.
Owls can turn their heads about 270 degrees, three-quarters of a full circle. That is far more than we can, because their eyes are fixed in place and they must turn the whole head to look around.

sec.h: Ears that see in the dark
sec.t:
Silent flight helps the owl hear as well as stay hidden. If its own wings were loud, it could not hear its prey. A barn owl's flat, heart-shaped face works like a satellite dish, gathering sound and funnelling it to the ears.

In barn owls, one ear opening sits higher on the head than the other. A sound from below reaches the lower ear a fraction louder. By comparing both ears, the owl can pinpoint a mouse up, down, left or right. In experiments in the USA, barn owls caught mice in total darkness using hearing alone. You use a simpler version of this trick to tell where a sound comes from, as explained in [[@ears-hear|how ears hear]].

In the 1990s, Japan's bullet trains had a noise problem. The pantograph, the arm on the roof that touches the overhead power line, howled as it cut through the air at high speed. An engineer named Eiji Nakatsu, who was also a [[@birdwatching|keen birdwatcher]], studied owl feathers. His team gave the pantograph small saw-tooth edges, a bit like the owl's comb. The train became noticeably quieter.

{{story:bullet-trains}}

Owls usually swallow small prey whole. Their stomachs digest the soft parts, but fur, feathers and bones are packed into a neat bundle called a pellet. A few hours later the owl coughs it up. Scientists collect owl pellets from under roosts to find out exactly what owls eat. Many classrooms in America and Europe pull them apart with tweezers and find tiny skulls and jaws inside.

Barn owls live on every continent except Antarctica, including all over India. Farmers sometimes welcome them, because a single family of barn owls can eat many rats and mice in one breeding season.

Owls have been given very different meanings around the world. In [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]], the little owl was linked with Athena, goddess of wisdom, and many Western [[@picture-books|picture books]] still show owls as wise. In India, the owl is the vahana, or vehicle, of the goddess Lakshmi, who is worshipped at [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]]. Yet "ullu" is also a playful Hindi word for a silly person.

Not all owls are silent. Fish owls, found in India and other parts of Asia, have lost most of the silent features, because fish cannot hear wings above the water. Silence, it turns out, is only worth having if your dinner can hear you coming. The soft feathers themselves have a long history, which you can trace in [[@feathers|where feathers came from]]. And bats, which hunt using sound in a very different way, are explained in [[@echolocation|echolocation]].

text: Sea salt is made by letting the sun and wind dry up seawater. Workers let seawater flow into a series of wide, shallow ponds called salt pans. As water [[evaporation|evaporates]], the water left behind gets saltier and saltier. Eventually it can hold no more salt, and white [[crystal|crystals]] begin to form on the bottom.

Salt workers then rake the crystals into piles, let them drain and dry, and send them off to be cleaned and packed. The whole process can take weeks, and it works best in places with hot sun, steady wind and little rain, such as the coasts of Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.

sec.t:
Seawater is about 3.5 percent salt. That doesn't sound like much, but it means each litre carries about 35 g, mostly sodium chloride, the same salt you sprinkle on food. Rivers wash tiny amounts of minerals off rocks into the sea, and over millions of years [[@why-sea-salty|the ocean has grown salty]].

In a salt works, seawater moves slowly from one pond to the next. In the first ponds, mud and sand settle out. Some minerals, such as gypsum, crystallise before common salt does. Only when the water has shrunk to about a tenth of its starting amount does sodium chloride start to form crystals. Workers try to collect the salt before other bitter-tasting minerals come out too.

sec.h: A handful of salt and a march
sec.t:
Salt has always mattered, because people need it to stay healthy and to preserve food. In British India, it was illegal for Indians to make or sell their own salt, and a tax was charged on it.

In 1930, Mahatma Gandhi and his followers walked about 385 km from Sabarmati Ashram to the seaside village of Dandi in Gujarat. On 6 April he picked up a lump of natural salt from the shore, breaking the law on purpose. The [[@salt-march|Salt March]] inspired people across India to make their own salt and helped build the movement for independence.

Salt pans can look surprisingly colourful. As brine gets saltier, it suits different tiny living things. A kind of green alga thrives in fairly salty water and turns orange-red as the salt increases. In the saltiest ponds, [[microbe|microbes]] stain the water pink or deep red.

From a plane over the south of [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]] Bay, old salt ponds look like a giant paint palette. Many of these ponds are now being turned back into [[wetland|wetlands]] for birds and fish. Some flamingos in India's salt flats and [[lagoon|lagoons]] feed on tiny brine shrimp that also live in very salty water.

text: Night animals see in the dark by catching every scrap of light they can. Many have huge eyes with wide pupils that let in more light. The back of their eyes, the [[retina|retina]], is packed with rod cells, which work well in dim light. And many have a mirror-like layer behind the retina that bounces light back for a second chance to be seen.

Even so, no animal can see in total darkness. Night animals also rely on other senses. Owls and foxes listen. Bats use [[echolocation|echoes]]. Some snakes sense the heat of a warm body. A night animal's world is built from many senses at once.

st.reveal: Behind the light-sensing layer of the eye, many night animals have a shiny layer called the tapetum lucidum. Light that passes through once gets bounced back for a second chance to be seen. Some of it escapes back out, which is the glow you see.

sec.t:
The bigger the eye, the more light it can gather. The tarsier, a tiny primate from Southeast Asia, has eyes so large that each one is about as big as its brain. It can't move them, so like an [[@owl-eyes|owl]] it turns its head instead.

India has its own big-eyed night specialist. The slender loris, a small, slow-moving primate found in southern India and Sri Lanka, creeps along branches at night hunting insects. Its round, staring eyes take up much of its face.

Pupils matter too. A cat's pupils close to narrow slits in sunlight to protect the eye, then open into wide circles at night. That lets them work well across a huge range of brightness.

For a long time, scientists thought that seeing colour at night was impossible. In dim light, people see mostly in shades of grey. Then, in 2002, a team in Sweden tested elephant hawkmoths. The moths could pick out coloured flowers by starlight.

Later, the same group found that some geckos can also see colour in light too dim for human colour vision. Their eyes work differently from ours, with larger light-catching cells.

There is a trade-off. Eyes tuned for the dark are often less sharp in daylight, and many night animals see fewer colours than we do. Being active at night has rewards that make up for it: cooler air in hot places like the Thar Desert, fewer daytime hunters and less competition for food.

[[@bats-fly|Bats]] hunt by sending out squeaks and listening for echoes. Pythons and pit vipers have small pits on their faces that sense [[infrared|infrared]] heat from warm-blooded prey. Cats sweep their whiskers to feel gaps and objects. Kiwis in New Zealand sniff for worms through nostrils at the tip of their beaks.

Night animals live closer to people than you might think. [[@leopards-cities|Leopards prowl]] the forest of Sanjay Gandhi National Park on the edge of [[@mumbai|Mumbai]]. In American cities, raccoons and opossums raid bins after dark. In many places, a [[@cats-domestic|cat]] on a wall at midnight is the night animal you are most likely to meet.

text: The mantis shrimp punches hard because its arm works like a loaded catapult. Its muscles slowly squeeze a spring inside the arm while a latch holds it back. When the latch lets go, the club-shaped arm shoots forward at about 80 km/h in water, as fast as a car on a highway.

That speed, packed into a body about 10 to 15 cm long, smashes the hard shells of snails, crabs and clams. The punch is so fast it creates collapsing bubbles that strike the prey again a split second later. Few animals of any size can match it.

sec.t:
Mantis shrimps are crustaceans, related to [[@crabs|crabs]], lobsters and real shrimps, but they belong to their own group. There are about 450 [[species|species]]. They live mostly in warm, shallow seas, including around [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]] and along India's coasts.

Scientists sort them into two kinds. "Spearers" have sharp, spiny arms to stab soft fish. "Smashers" have heavy, hammer-like clubs to break shells. The peacock mantis shrimp, with its bright green, red and blue colours, is the most famous smasher.

The club moves so fast that water can't keep up behind it. The pressure drops so low that the water briefly turns into vapour bubbles, a process called cavitation.

These bubbles collapse almost at once. As they do, they release a burst of energy, a tiny flash of light and heat of thousands of degrees for a fraction of a second. So the prey gets hit twice: first by the club, then by the shock of the collapsing bubbles. Even if the club misses, the bubbles can stun.

A punch like that should shatter the club itself. Yet a mantis shrimp can strike thousands of times between moults. Its club is built in layers of fibres twisted in a spiral pattern, like stacks of plywood turned slightly each time. When a crack starts, it has to twist round and round the layers instead of running straight through.

Engineers are copying this design to make lighter, tougher helmets, armour and aeroplane parts.

The mantis shrimp also has some of the strangest eyes on Earth. Humans have three types of colour [[receptor|receptors]]. Mantis shrimps have 12 or more. They can see [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light and polarised light, which is light vibrating in a particular direction.

Each eye moves on its own stalk and can judge distance without the other. Scientists think their eyes help them spot prey, rivals and mates in a flash.

Aquarium keepers tell stories of mantis shrimps cracking glass tanks, which is why some are kept behind thick acrylic. Divers call them "thumb splitters" because a careless hand can be badly cut.

Another small sea creature uses bubbles as a weapon too. The [[@power-pistol-shrimp|pistol shrimp]] snaps its claw shut so fast that it fires a jet of water and makes one of the loudest sounds in the sea.

text: When a roller coaster goes round a loop, the track keeps forcing the train, and you, to change direction. You want to keep going straight, but the track bends you into a curve. That pushes you firmly into your seat.

At the top of the loop, [[gravity|gravity]] is pulling you down towards the ground. But if the train is moving fast enough, the track has to push you down even harder than gravity alone to keep you on the curve. So gravity is not enough to pull you away from the seat. You stay pressed in, even upside down.
If the train went too slowly, gravity would win. That's why designers calculate the speed very carefully.

st.prompt: Why are modern coaster loops shaped like an upside-down teardrop instead of a circle?

options.t: A tighter top and gentler sides keep the forces on riders comfortable
Teardrops are cheaper to build than circles
The shape makes the ride last longer

st.reveal: On a circular loop, the train has to enter very fast to make it over the top, which squashes riders hard at the bottom. A teardrop loop curves gently where the train is fast and tightly where it is slow, so the push on riders stays safer.

sec.t:
Swing a bucket of water fast in a big vertical circle and the water stays in, even upside down. Swing it slowly and it pours on your head.

The water wants to fly off in a straight line. The bucket keeps getting in its way, pushing it round. As long as the bucket swings fast enough, it pushes the water harder than [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] pulls it, and the water stays put. Scientists call the inward push that keeps something moving in a curve a centripetal force.

A coaster car is the bucket, and you are the water.

sec.h: Squashed at the bottom, light at the top

sec.t:
People tried loops long ago. In 1895, the Flip Flap Railway at Coney Island in New York sent riders round a perfect circle. To get over the top, cars had to enter very fast. At the bottom of the circle, the sudden curve slammed riders with huge forces, and many complained of neck pain. Loops fell out of fashion for decades.

The fix came from a change of shape. A teardrop loop, called a clothoid, is tall and narrow. It curves gently at the bottom, where the train is fast, and tightly at the top, where it is slow. That keeps forces safer. In 1976, the Revolution at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California became one of the first modern coasters with a loop like this, and loops took off again.

sec.h: Speed, height and the first drop
sec.t:
Most coasters have no engine on the train. A chain or a launch system pulls it up to the top of the first hill. After that, it is gravity all the way. The height of that first hill sets the energy for the whole ride, which is why every later hill and loop must be lower.

The fastest coaster in the world in 2026 is Falcon's Flight in Saudi Arabia, which opened on the last day of 2025 and reaches about 250 km/h. That is about twice the top speed of most Indian express trains. Before it, Formula Rossa in Abu Dhabi held the record for years, at about 240 km/h. India has big coasters too, at parks near Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

Each lap also loses a little energy to [[@friction|friction]] with the rails and pushing through air. Engineers plan for that, so the train has just enough speed left to coast safely into the station.

At the very top of the first drop, before the train plunges, riders get a flash of floating weightlessness. Skydivers feel it for the first few seconds after they leap, until the rushing air builds up and, in a real [[@sky-skydiving|skydive]], holds them up like a soft hand.

text: Almost everything made by people was designed by someone. Industrial or product designers plan the shape of objects like chairs, kettles, phones and toothbrushes. Graphic designers create logos, signs, posters and [[@life-money-world|the symbols on money]]. UX designers (UX stands for user experience) work out how apps and websites should work, so they feel easy.

Designers think about how people will use something, what it should be made of, how it can be built cheaply and safely, and how it looks. When design is good, you hardly notice it. When it is bad, you push a door that should be pulled, or lose your way in an app.

st.prompt: You walk up to a glass door with a big handle on both sides. You pull, but it only opens if you push. Whose fault is it, according to designers?

st.reveal: Designers say a good object shows you how to use it. A handle invites pulling, while a flat plate invites pushing. Doors that confuse people are sometimes nicknamed "Norman doors", after the designer Don Norman, who wrote about them.

d.try: Pick one everyday object at home, such as a water bottle, a school bag or a TV remote. Write down three things that are annoying about it. Then draw a better version that fixes them, and test your idea by asking a family member how they would use it.
myth: Design is just about making things look pretty.
Looks matter, but most design is about how something works, how easy it is to use and how safe it is. A well-designed object often feels so natural that you don't notice the design at all.

sec.t:
In 1988 the American scientist Don Norman wrote a book now known as *The Design of Everyday Things*. Its first edition had a slightly different title, *The Psychology of Everyday Things*. His big idea was that objects should show you how to use them, without needing instructions.

A button that sticks up says "press me". A handle says "pull me". A flat metal plate on a door says "push here". When an object sends the wrong message, people blame themselves, but Norman said the real fault usually lies with the design. Confusing doors are now jokingly called "Norman doors".

Good designers try to make things that work for as many people as possible, including children, older people and people with disabilities. This is called universal or inclusive design.

Kerb ramps at street corners were made for wheelchair users, but they also help people with prams, suitcases and bicycles. Large, soft-grip kitchen tools were first designed for people with stiff hands, and many others found them easier too. Ideas like these come up again and again when people think about how the world can [[@disabilities-inclusion|work better for everyone]].

In 1958 the Government of India invited two famous American designers, Charles and Ray Eames, to travel around India and suggest how to train designers. They admired the humble *lota*, the round brass water pot, saying its shape had been perfected over centuries of use.

Their report led to the National Institute of Design in [[@ahmedabad|Ahmedabad]], founded in 1961. Its graduates now design everything from buses to banknotes.

Until 2010, the Indian rupee had no symbol of its own. The government held a competition, and thousands of people sent in ideas. The winner was D. Udaya Kumar, then a postgraduate student at IIT Bombay.

His ₹ blends the Devanagari letter "र" (ra) with the Roman letter "R". The two lines across the top suggest India's flag, and the gap between the top line and the letter below hints at the equals sign, standing for balance. It now appears on [[@money-worth|banknotes]], coins, price tags and phone keyboards everywhere.

Today many designers [[@screen-design|work on screens]]. They decide where buttons go in an app, what happens when you tap, and how to show information clearly. They test early versions with real users and change what confuses them, the same way [[@apps-made|app makers]] test new features. A good app, like a good door handle, should make you feel clever without ever explaining itself.

text: A handful of paintings are known almost everywhere. Leonardo da Vinci's *Mona Lisa*, Vincent van Gogh's *The Starry Night*, Johannes Vermeer's *Girl with a Pearl Earring* and Pablo Picasso's *Guernica* are among them. So is *The Great Wave off Kanagawa*, a Japanese print by Katsushika Hokusai.

None of them became famous only because it was beautiful. A painting usually needs a good story too: a theft, a tragic artist, a war, or an image so simple it can be printed on anything, from posters to coffee mugs. In the last 150 years, [[@photography-history|photography]] and printing have spread these images far beyond the museums that own them.

st.prompt: Why are there thousands of "original" copies of Hokusai's Great Wave in museums around the world?

options.t: It is a woodblock print, made to be printed many times
Hokusai painted it again every day of his life
Museums secretly swapped copies for the real one

st.reveal: The Great Wave was carved into wooden blocks and printed in large numbers to sell cheaply in Japan. Thousands were made, so many museums own a genuine early print.

d.try: Pick a painting you like from a library book or a museum website. Spend two full minutes looking at it without talking, then list ten things you noticed. Ask a friend to do the same with the same picture and compare your lists. Most people are surprised how different they are.
myth: The Mona Lisa's eyes follow you around the room because Leonardo used a secret trick.
Almost any portrait where the subject looks straight out at the painter seems to follow you as you move. It is an effect of how our brains read a flat picture, not a hidden technique.

sec.t:
The [[@mona-lisa|Mona Lisa]] was painted in the early 1500s and probably shows Lisa Gherardini, the wife of a merchant in Florence. For centuries it was admired by artists, but it was not world-famous.

Then, in August 1911, an Italian handyman named Vincenzo Peruggia, who had worked at the Louvre, hid in the museum and walked out with it. The theft made headlines around the world. Crowds queued to stare at the empty space on the wall. When the painting was found in Italy two years later, it came home a celebrity. Today millions of people visit the Louvre each year, and many of them head straight for it.

In April 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, the town of Guernica in northern Spain was bombed from the air. Many civilians died. Picasso, living in Paris, painted *Guernica* in response.

It is huge, almost 8 m wide, about as long as three autorickshaws parked end to end, and painted only in black, white and grey. It shows a screaming horse, a bull, a mother holding her child, and broken figures. There is no blood and no planes, yet people find it hard to look away. It has become one of the world's best-known pictures about the suffering of war.

sec.h: A girl, a wave, and many more
sec.t:
Vermeer's *Girl with a Pearl Earring*, painted around 1665, shows a girl turning to look over her shoulder. Nobody knows who she was, and that mystery is part of its pull. It hangs in the Mauritshuis museum in The Hague, in the Netherlands.

Hokusai's *Great Wave*, from about 1831, shows a giant wave curling over boats, with [[@mount-fuji|Mount Fuji]] small in the distance. It was printed from wooden blocks, a bit like the [[@printing-press|printing press]] printed books, so thousands of copies were made.

India has its own famous paintings, too. [[@raja-ravi-varma|Raja Ravi Varma]]'s goddesses were printed in huge numbers and hung in homes across the country. [[@amrita-sher-gil|Amrita Sher-Gil]]'s *Three Girls* (1935) is one of the best-known works of modern Indian art. Which painting counts as "most famous" depends a lot on where you grew up.

text: A piano is a box of strings that are hit by hammers. When you press a key, it works like a seesaw. The far end of the key rises and flicks a small felt-covered hammer up towards the strings. The hammer strikes, then drops back at once so the strings can ring.

The vibrating strings are thin, so on their own they would be quiet. They pass their [[vibration|vibrations]] to a large, thin wooden sheet called the soundboard, which shakes a great deal of air. That is what you hear. Let go of the key, and a felt pad called a damper falls onto the strings to stop the sound.

st.prompt: When you press a piano key, what makes the sound?

options.t: A felt-covered hammer hits the strings
Air rushes through a pipe
A small hook plucks a string

st.reveal: Each key is a lever that throws a felt hammer up at the strings. A small hook plucking a string is how the older harpsichord works, and air through a pipe is how an organ works.

src: Britannica, Piano.
Rossing T.D. (2014) Springer Handbook of Acoustics.

d.try: Stretch a few rubber bands around an open box. Pluck one with your finger, then tap it with the rubber end of a pencil. Plucking is how a harpsichord makes sound, and striking is how a piano does it. Listen for which sound is softer and which is sharper.
myth: The piano is a string instrument, so it has nothing in common with drums.
The piano's sound comes from strings, but they are struck by hammers, as a drum is struck. That is why music experts often describe the piano as both a string and a percussion instrument.

sec.h: A piano is full of levers
sec.t:
Each key is a [[@lever-lift|lever]], and behind it sits a clever set of more [[lever|levers]] called the action. A grand piano's action has dozens of small wooden and felt parts for each key.

The trickiest part is called the escapement. As the hammer nears the string, it is set free and flies the last bit on its own. If it stayed pushed against the string, it would stop the note dead. Thanks to the escapement, a pianist can repeat a note very fast and play from a whisper to a crash.

A concert grand piano has about 230 strings. The low notes use one or two thick strings wrapped in copper wire. Most middle and high notes use three thinner steel strings tuned to exactly the same note, which makes them louder.

Together, the strings pull on the frame with a force of around 20 tonnes, close to the weight of a loaded lorry. Early wooden frames couldn't take this, so modern pianos have a heavy cast-iron frame. That is one reason a concert grand weighs about half a tonne, as much as seven or eight grown-ups. Shorter, thinner strings vibrate faster and make higher notes, as explained in [[@sound-travel|sound travel]].

When [[@mozart|Mozart]] was writing music in the 1780s, his piano had a range of about five [[octave|octaves]], about 61 notes. Composers kept wanting more notes and more power. [[@beethoven|Beethoven]] wrote music that seemed to push his pianos to breaking point, and makers responded with stronger frames and extra keys.

By the late 1800s, the 88-key piano had become standard. Companies like Steinway, founded in [[@new-york|New York]] in 1853, built pianos for concert halls and for millions of homes. For a time, owning a piano in the parlour was a sign of a comfortable American family.

Pianos arrived in India with Europeans and were found in [[colonial|colonial]] homes, schools and churches. Many older Hindi films have scenes of a hero singing at a piano.

Today, the piano is one of the most popular instruments for children to learn, from Mumbai to Minneapolis. Many homes now have digital pianos, which use recorded sounds of real piano notes instead of strings. They are lighter and cheaper, and they never need tuning, but pianists can still feel the difference.

text: For more than two thousand years, Indian cloth was some of the most wanted in the world. Indian weavers made cotton so fine it floated like mist, and dyers made colours that stayed bright after washing. Traders carried Indian [[textile|textiles]] to Rome, Egypt, China, Southeast Asia, Africa and Europe.

Indian cotton changed what the world wore. Even the English language is full of words for cloth that came from India. The story also has a hard side. When British factories began making cheap cloth with machines, India's handweavers suffered badly, and that became a big part of [[@freedom-struggle|India's freedom struggle]].

st.prompt: Why were European buyers so excited by Indian printed cotton in the 1600s?

options.t: Its bright colours stayed bright even after washing
It was the only cloth that was waterproof
It glowed in the dark

st.reveal: Most European dyes of the time faded or ran in the wash. Indian dyers had perfected ways to fix colours into cotton using mordants, so reds, blues and yellows survived many washes. That felt like a small miracle to buyers.

d.try: Ask an adult if you can look at the labels on clothes and sheets at home. Make a list of the fabrics and the countries they were made in. How many say cotton? How many come from India? Then look up where cotton plants grow.
myth: Fine cotton cloth was a European invention of the Industrial Revolution.

Indian weavers had been making fine cotton cloth for thousands of years. British factories in the 1700s and 1800s mostly copied Indian designs and used machines to make similar cloth faster and cheaper.
facts: named from a Greek word meaning Indian

sec.t:
India is one of the first places where people grew cotton and spun it into thread. At Mohenjo-daro, one of the great [[@indus-cities|Indus Valley cities]], [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found a scrap of cotton cloth over 4,000 years old. It had been dyed red with madder, a plant root.

Cotton is tricky to spin, because its fibres are short. Indian spinners learned to twist them into long, strong threads by hand. Weavers then turned that thread into cloth on wooden [[loom|looms]].

Indian dyers were masters of colour. They used plants like indigo for blue, madder for red and [[@turmeric|turmeric]] or pomegranate rind for yellow. The secret was the [[mordant|mordant]], a substance that helps dye bond to cotton. With mordants, Indian colours stayed bright after many washes.

Indigo was so linked with India that its name comes from a Greek word meaning "Indian". When Europeans saw [[@kalamkari|printed and painted Indian cottons]] in the 1600s, they went wild for them. They called them calico, after the [[@sea-ports|port of Calicut]] (Kozhikode), and chintz, from the Hindi word *chhint*, meaning spotted or sprinkled.

The [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] shipped huge amounts of Indian cotton to Britain. Soon everyone wanted calico curtains, dresses and bedspreads. British wool and silk weavers were furious. In 1700 and 1721, Parliament passed laws that banned importing or wearing most printed Indian cottons.

British inventors then built machines to spin and weave cotton cheaply, a key part of the [[@industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]]. Raw cotton was shipped from India to British mills, and machine-made cloth was sold back to India.

Machine-made cloth was cheaper than handwoven cloth. Under British rule, Indian weavers could not compete, and many lost their living. Towns that had been famous for [[weaving|weaving]] shrank.

In the early 1900s, leaders of the freedom movement urged Indians to buy Indian cloth instead of British. [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] went further, spinning his own thread and asking everyone to wear handmade khadi. Today India's [[@knitting-weaving|handloom weavers]] still make famous fabrics, from [[@art-banarasi|Banarasi silk]] to [[@art-ikat|Pochampally ikat]], and many of them have legal protection for their names.

text: A discount is a cut in price, usually written as a [[percentage|percentage]]. "25% off" means you take away a quarter of the price. On a ₹400 book, that's ₹100 off, so you pay ₹300. On a $40 game, it's $10 off.

The maths is simple when there's one discount. It gets tricky when shops stack them, mix them with free gifts or hide them behind words like "up to". That's not an accident. Shops know that a big, round number grabs attention faster than a careful sum.
Learning a few tricks with [[@percentages|percentages]] lets you see straight through most of them.

st.prompt: A ₹1,000 jacket is marked 20% off. At the till, you get an extra 10% off. What do you pay?
st.reveal: 20% off ₹1,000 brings it to ₹800. The extra 10% is taken from ₹800, not ₹1,000, so it removes ₹80. You pay ₹720, which is 28% off in total.

src: Government of India, Department of Consumer Affairs, Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011.
Federal Trade Commission (USA), Guides Against Deceptive Pricing.

d.try: Collect three sale leaflets or online offers. For each one, work out the actual price in rupees or dollars and the real total percentage off. Then rank them from best deal to worst and see whether the one that looked biggest really was.
myth: 50% off plus an extra 20% off means 70% off.
The second discount is taken from the already reduced price. Half of ₹1,000 is ₹500, and 20% of ₹500 is ₹100, so you pay ₹400. That's 60% off, not 70%.
facts: the same as 50% off each item, if you wanted two

sec.t:
Say a shoe shop offers 50% off, plus an extra 20% at the till. It sounds like 70% off. It isn't.

The first discount turns ₹2,000 into ₹1,000. The second takes 20% of ₹1,000, which is ₹200. You pay ₹800, so you saved 60%. Each new discount works on a smaller number, so the total is always less than simply adding the percentages.

There's a quick way to check. Turn each discount into what you *keep*: 50% off means you pay 0.5, and 20% off means you pay 0.8. Multiply them: 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4. You pay 40% of the price. The same trick works for any pair of discounts.

sec.h: What price are they cutting from?
sec.t:
A discount is only as honest as the price it starts from. In India, packaged goods must show an MRP, the maximum retail price, and shops may not charge more than that. It's one of the basic [[@consumer-rights|consumer rights]] every shopper has. A sale is usually measured against the MRP.

In the USA there's no MRP. Shops set their own prices, and the government's Federal Trade Commission warns against fake "was" prices that the item never really sold at. There's another twist for American shoppers: in most states, sales [[@taxes|tax]] is added at the till. A $20 shirt "on sale" may cost more like $21.50 once tax goes on. Five states have no statewide sales tax at all.

Prices like ₹499 or $9.99 are called charm pricing. We read numbers from the left, so ₹499 feels closer to ₹400 than to ₹500, even though it's just one rupee short. In India you'll see ₹999 and ₹1,499 everywhere, and in the USA prices like $19.99 are so common that a round $20 can look odd. Studies of shoppers have found that these prices often do sell more.

[[@advertising|Advertisers]] also use red tags, countdown clocks and words like "last chance". Big sales cluster around festivals: Diwali in India, and Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, in the USA.

Before you buy, ask two questions. What will I actually pay, in rupees or dollars? Would I buy this at that price if there were no sale sign? If the answer to the second question is no, the best discount is 100%, and you keep all your money.

text: Growing pains are aches in the legs that many children get, usually between about 3 and 12 years old. They tend to come in the late afternoon, evening or night, often in both legs, in the calves, the fronts of the thighs or behind the knees. Some nights the ache is strong enough to wake a child up. By morning it's gone.
Despite the name, doctors don't think growing causes them. Nobody knows the exact cause. The good news is that growing pains are harmless, leave no lasting damage and fade as children get older.

st.prompt: Which of these is typical of ordinary growing pains?

options.t: Aching in both legs in the evening, gone by morning
Pain in one swollen knee that lasts all day
A limp along with a fever

st.reveal: Growing pains usually affect both legs, come in the evening or night and are gone by morning. Pain in just one spot, swelling, limping or fever are not typical and need a doctor to check.

Nemours KidsHealth, growing pains.

n.certNote: Doctors agree growing pains are common and harmless. Their cause is unknown. Leading ideas include tired muscles after an active day and a lower pain threshold, but none is proven.

d.try: Learn a simple calf stretch. Stand facing a wall with your hands on it, one foot forward and one back. Keep your back heel on the floor and lean forward gently until you feel a stretch in the back leg. Hold for 15 seconds, then swap legs. Some children find stretching before bed helps.
myth: Growing pains are caused by bones growing faster than the body can handle.
Bones grow slowly and steadily, and growing pains don't match times of fast growth. They also happen in muscles, not in bones or joints. The name has stuck even though the explanation hasn't.

estimates range from about 1 in 10 to 1 in 3 children

sec.t:
In 1823, the French doctor Marcel Duchamp wrote about children with aches he called "douleurs de croissance", or pains of growth. The name was catchy and spread around the world.

But it doesn't hold up well. [[@bones-growth|Bones grow]] slowly and steadily through childhood, with the fastest growth in babyhood and during the [[@body-growth-spurts|teenage growth spurt]]. Growing pains are most common in the years between, and nobody has found that children with them grow faster. The aches are also felt in [[@muscles|muscles]], not at the ends of bones where growth happens.

Doctors have several ideas, and the answer might be a mix.

One idea is simple tiredness. Growing pains often come after a day full of running, jumping and climbing, a bit like the ache adults feel after unusual exercise. Another is that some children are more sensitive to [[@pain|pain]] in general. Growing pains also tend to run in families. A few studies have looked at whether low [[vitamin|vitamin]] D or less-dense bones play a part, but the results aren't clear yet.

Researchers in Australia found in 2004 that over a third of children aged 4 to 6 in their study had pains matching the description. Other studies give lower figures, partly because doctors don't all define growing pains the same way.

{{story:sports-science}}

Growing pains usually go away by themselves, and there are simple things that can make a bad night easier. Many children find that gentle massage of the sore legs by a parent helps. Warmth, like a warm wheat bag or a warm bath, can relax the muscles.

Stretching the calves and thighs, especially before bed, helps some children. Athletes use similar stretches, and [[@sports-science|sports scientists]] study how stretching and rest help muscles recover. If the pain is bad, a parent can ask a doctor or pharmacist what else might help.

Growing pains have a typical pattern, and doctors check for anything that doesn't fit it. Tell a parent or trusted adult if the pain is in only one leg or one spot, or in a joint like the knee or ankle. Swelling, redness or limping are other reasons to speak up. So is pain during the day that stops you playing, a fever, or feeling unwell in other ways.

These signs don't usually mean anything serious, but they do mean a doctor should take a look. Growing pains are what doctors call a diagnosis of exclusion: they decide it's growing pains once they've ruled other causes out.

Most children stop getting growing pains by their early teenage years, often well before. Anyone woken up by aching legs can take comfort that they leave no lasting harm. Plenty of adults remember them, and plenty of children who had them go on to run marathons, dance and play every sport there is.

text: A deepfake is a video, picture or sound recording that has been made or changed by [[@ai-art|artificial intelligence]] to show someone doing or saying something they never did. It might swap one person's face onto another's body, make a politician appear to give a speech, or [[@tech-voice-cloning|copy a relative's voice]] on the phone.

The name mixes "deep learning", a powerful kind of AI, with "fake". Deepfakes can be fun or useful, in films and games for example. They can also be used to trick, bully or spread lies, which is why it helps to know how they work.

st.prompt: How much recorded speech can some modern tools need to copy a person's voice convincingly?

options.t: Hundreds of hours
As little as a few seconds to a minute
It cannot be done at all

st.reveal: Newer voice-cloning tools can imitate someone from very short clips, such as a video posted online. That is why some families agree on a secret code word to check a caller is really who they say they are.

d.try: Agree on a family "safe word" that only you and your parents know. If anyone ever calls or messages claiming to be a family member in trouble, asking for the safe word is a quick way to check. Practise it once so everyone remembers.
myth: You can always spot a deepfake if you look closely, for example by checking whether the person blinks.

Early deepfakes had giveaways like strange blinking, but newer ones fix many of those flaws, and even experts can be fooled. Checking where a video came from, and whether trusted news sources report it, is more reliable than staring at pixels.
facts: deep learning, a kind of artificial intelligence
check the source, not just the picture

sec.t:
To make a face-swap video, a computer studies hundreds or thousands of pictures of two people. It learns to describe each face as a set of features, such as the shape of the mouth, the angle of the head, and the expression. Then it redraws person A's features on person B, frame by frame, so the new face moves and talks in time.

One clever design, invented in 2014, uses two programs that compete. One, the generator, makes fakes. The other, the discriminator, tries to spot them. Each round, the generator learns from its mistakes, and the fakes get better and better. These are called generative adversarial networks.

The same tools power some exciting work. Filmmakers use them to make actors look younger, or to bring back a character after an actor has died, with permission from the family. [[@dubbing-subtitles|Dubbing]] studios can match an actor's lip movements to a new language, so a film dubbed into Hindi looks as if it was shot in Hindi.

Voice technology can also help people who have lost their voice to illness, by recreating it from old recordings so they can still "speak" like themselves.

Deepfakes have been used to embarrass people, especially women and girls, and to spread false stories about politicians [[@election-commission|before elections]]. In 2023, after deepfake videos of Indian film stars spread online, India's government told [[@social-media|social media]] companies to remove such content quickly.

Many countries are writing new laws. Some require AI-made content to be labelled. Tech companies are also testing invisible watermarks that mark a picture or video as AI-made. None of these fixes is perfect yet.

Look for odd details, like blurry edges around the face, teeth that look strange, or lighting that doesn't match. But don't rely on that alone. Ask where the video came from. Is a trusted news organisation reporting it? Does it seem designed to make you angry or scared, fast?

If a message asks for money or secrets, check with a real person you trust, using a phone number you already know. The same questions that help you catch [[@fake-news|fake news]] work on deepfakes too. And never share a fake video of someone, even as a joke, because it can hurt them and may be against the law.

text: Flying cars already exist, in a way. Inventors have built cars that sprout wings, and small aircraft that can drive on roads, for almost a hundred years. Some have flown well.

What we don't have yet is the dream from cartoons: millions of people zipping over traffic jams in their own family car. That runs into big problems. Flying is far harder than driving, aircraft are expensive and noisy, and a crash in the air over a city is much more dangerous than a bump on the road.

The idea most likely to arrive soon is different. It is the air taxi, a small electric aircraft that takes off straight up like a [[@helicopters|helicopter]] and carries a few passengers across a city, flown by a trained pilot.

options.t: Many small electric motors are quieter and safer if one fails

st.reveal: Electric motors are light and simple, so designers can spread many around the aircraft. If one stops, the others can still land it safely. Smaller, slower-turning blades also make less of the loud thumping that helicopters are known for.

myth: Flying cars have never actually been built.
Dozens have been built and flown since the 1930s, and some have been certified to fly. The trouble is that most were expensive, noisy or awkward as both a car and a plane.

sec.t:
In 1937 an American inventor, Waldo Waterman, flew his Arrowbile, a car with detachable wings. In the 1940s and 1950s other roadable aircraft followed. One, the Aerocar, was approved to fly in the USA in 1956, but only a handful were built.

The problem was always the same. A good car needs to be heavy and strong to survive bumps. A good plane needs to be light. A machine that does both usually does both badly.

In 2021, a Slovakian inventor, Stefan Klein, flew his AirCar from the airport in Nitra to the airport in Bratislava in about 35 minutes. On landing, the wings folded away in a few minutes, and he drove into the city. It is a road car that can fly, but it still needs a runway.

New technology has changed the picture. Batteries and electric motors have become lighter and more powerful. Computers can keep a wobbly aircraft steady, as they do in [[@drones|drones]].

So many companies are building eVTOLs, which stands for electric vertical take-off and landing. Most look like a cross between a small plane and a giant drone. They have several [[propeller|propellers]] that tilt or lift, so they can rise straight up from a rooftop, then fly forward on wings.

Firms in the USA, Europe, China and India are testing them. In 2024 the US company Joby agreed with Dubai to start air taxi rides there, with first paying passengers planned for about 2026. In India, start-ups such as the ePlane Company, which began at IIT Madras, and Bengaluru's Sarla Aviation are designing air taxis for crowded cities.

{{story:jules-verne}}

Batteries are the biggest limit. They store far less energy for their weight than fuel does, so most air taxis can fly only short trips, often tens of kilometres, before recharging. That is fine for crossing a city, but not for a long journey.

Then there is safety. Every new aircraft must pass years of tests before passengers can ride in it. Cities would need landing pads called vertiports, and a new way to manage busy skies, a bit like [[@air-traffic|air traffic control]] for low-flying taxis.

Noise matters too. Electric air taxis are quieter than helicopters, but hundreds of them over a city would still be heard. And at first, rides are likely to cost much more than a cab.

Probably, but not quite the way old films showed it. For a while, flying taxis will most likely be a pricey extra in a few rich cities, with pilots on board and fixed routes between airports and city centres.

Later, if batteries improve and the aircraft prove safe, the price could fall and pilots might be replaced by computers. Some experts think that could take decades. Others think it will never be cheap enough for everyday use. Either way, the family car parked on the roof is still a long way off, and most of us will keep using roads, [[@metro-trains|metro trains]] and buses for years to come.

text: In 1905 the British government split the large province of Bengal into two. The eastern part, with a Muslim majority, joined Assam to form a new province with its capital at Dacca (now Dhaka). The western part, with a Hindu majority, stayed with Calcutta, now [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], as its capital, along with Bihar and Orissa.

The British said Bengal was simply too big to govern well. Many Indians believed the real aim was to weaken Bengal, the heart of the growing freedom movement, by splitting Hindus and Muslims. The [[partition|partition]] sparked huge protests and the [[@swadeshi|Swadeshi movement]]. In 1911 the British gave in and reunited Bengal.

options.t: The capital of India would move from Calcutta to Delhi
India would get full independence

st.reveal: At a grand ceremony in Delhi called the Delhi Durbar, King George V announced both changes. Moving the capital took power away from Calcutta, the centre of Bengali protest, even as the province was rejoined.

n.certNote: The events are well recorded. Historians still debate how much the partition was about running a huge province and how much it was meant to weaken Bengali nationalism by dividing Hindus and Muslims.

myth: The 1905 partition created the border between India and Bangladesh.

sec.t:
Bengal under British rule was enormous. It stretched over today's West Bengal, Bangladesh, Bihar, Jharkhand and Odisha, with about 7.8 crore people, more than most countries in Europe. Running it from Calcutta was hard, and the east, around Dacca, was often neglected.

Lord Curzon, the Viceroy, decided to divide it. Officials pointed to genuine problems with administration. But their private notes also show political aims. In 1904 a senior official, Herbert Risley, wrote that Bengal united was a power, and Bengal divided would pull in different ways.

Critics replied that Bengal could have been made smaller without splitting the Bengali-speaking people in two. One option was to separate off the regions where other languages, such as Hindi and Odia, were spoken. In the end, that is roughly what happened in 1911.

The partition came into force on 16 October 1905. In Calcutta, many people fasted, closed shops and walked to the river to bathe. Rabindranath Tagore led processions where Hindus and Muslims tied rakhis on each other's wrists, to show that Bengal could not be split.

Crowds sang "Vande Mataram". Students joined in large numbers. People boycotted British goods and burned foreign cloth. The protest spread to other parts of India, led by figures such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Lala Lajpat Rai.

The protests also produced songs that are still sung today. Tagore wrote "Amar Sonar Bangla", meaning "My golden Bengal", in 1905. Painters, poets and playwrights joined in, and shops selling only Indian-made goods opened in Calcutta's markets.

{{story:bangladesh}}

Not everyone opposed the partition. Many Muslim leaders in eastern Bengal welcomed it. The new province gave Dacca new offices, schools and jobs, and Muslims there, many of them poor farmers, had a larger voice.

In 1906 the All-India Muslim League was founded at a meeting in Dacca. Some historians see the partition and the arguments over it as an early step in the split between Hindu and Muslim politics that shaped the [[subcontinent|subcontinent]] later. Others warn against reading the future back into 1905.

In December 1911, King George V visited India for a ceremony called the Delhi Durbar. The Durbar was a vast gathering on open ground in north Delhi, with tens of thousands of people. Princes came in jewels, and the king and queen sat on thrones under a golden dome. There he announced that Bengal would be reunited. Bihar and Orissa became a separate province, and Assam went back to being separate too.

He also announced that the capital of British India would move from Calcutta to [[@delhi|Delhi]]. That ended Calcutta's long role as capital. Many Muslims in the east felt let down by the reversal.

Bengal was divided again in 1947, during the [[@partition|Partition]] of India, when East Bengal became part of Pakistan. In 1971, after a war, it became the independent country of [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]], whose anthem is a Tagore song written in 1905.

text: Howrah Bridge is a giant steel bridge across the Hooghly River, joining the city of Howrah to [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] in West Bengal. It opened in 1943 and is one of the busiest bridges in the world.

It is special for several reasons. It is a cantilever bridge, with no pillars in the river between its two big towers, so ships could pass freely. It was built without nuts and bolts, held together by rivets. And it was made almost entirely of Indian steel, during the Second World War.
Since 1965 its official name has been Rabindra Setu, after the poet [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]]. Most people still call it Howrah Bridge.

st.reveal: It is a cantilever bridge. Each tower holds out a huge arm, balanced by a shorter anchor arm on the land side. A middle section hangs between the two arms, like two people reaching out and holding a plank between their hands.

sec.t:
In the 1800s Calcutta, as Kolkata was then called, was the capital of British India and one of the busiest ports in Asia. Howrah, across the river, had the big railway station.

In 1874 a pontoon bridge was opened between them. It floated on boats and had to be opened in the middle to let ships through, stopping all traffic. As the cities grew, it became hopelessly crowded.

A new fixed bridge was planned. The river was busy with ships and the riverbed was soft, so engineers chose a design with no supports in the water at all.

Work started in the late 1930s, with a firm called Braithwaite, Burn and Jessop Construction Company doing the building. The Second World War broke out in 1939. Steel from Britain became hard to get.

So the builders turned to Tata Steel in Jamshedpur. Of about 26,500 tonnes of [[@steel|steel]] in the bridge, around 23,000 tonnes was a special high-strength kind made by Tata.

The bridge opened to traffic in February 1943, with no grand ceremony. Japan's armies were then fighting in nearby Burma, and the city feared air raids. The [[@world-war-two|war]] shaped the bridge from start to finish.

Howrah Bridge is about 705 m long. Its main span, the part between the two towers, is about 457 m, longer than four football fields placed end to end.

Each tower holds out a long arm over the river, balanced by a shorter arm on the land side, like a see-saw. The two river arms don't meet directly. A middle section hangs between them. Together they make one smooth line across the water.

The whole steel frame is joined with rivets, hot metal pins hammered flat at each end. Rivets were the usual way to build big steel structures then, but people still marvel that such a giant has no nuts or bolts.

{{story:golden-gate}}

Every day, huge numbers of people cross. Estimates from the 2010s put it at around a lakh vehicles and well over a lakh people on foot, along with handcarts, cycles and porters carrying loads on their heads.

Beneath it, ferries cross the river and the busy Mallik Ghat flower market spreads along the bank. At night the bridge is lit up, and it has starred in many Bengali and Hindi films.

The bridge's toughest enemy turned out to be people. Many travellers chew paan or gutkha, a tobacco mixture, and spit the red juice on the bridge. The juice mixed with rain made the steel at the base of the pillars [[@rust|rust]] and thin out.

Around 2011 engineers found that some steel covers had lost about half their thickness. The port fixed the damage and wrapped the pillar bases in fibreglass to protect them. Signs now ask people not to spit.

Today the bridge is more than 80 years old. Newer bridges, such as [[@ishwar-chandra|Vidyasagar Setu]], carry some of the load, but Howrah Bridge is still the most famous crossing in Kolkata.

text: Sikkim, a small state in the eastern Himalaya, decided in 2003 to stop using chemical [[fertiliser|fertilisers]] and [[pesticide|pesticides]] on its farms. Over the next 12 years, the government cut and then banned their sale, trained farmers in natural methods, and paid for farmland to be checked and certified. In January 2016, Sikkim was declared fully organic.

Organic farming means growing food without factory-made chemical fertilisers or pesticides. Instead, farmers feed the [[@soil-made|soil]] with [[compost|compost]] and manure, and keep pests down with natural sprays, crop rotation and helpful insects. Sikkim's leaders wanted to protect its mountain soils, rivers and forests, and to earn more from food sold as pure and healthy.

st.reveal: Organic farmers return nutrients to the soil with compost, cow dung, leaf litter and vermicompost made by earthworms. They also grow crops like beans, which add nitrogen to the soil naturally.

Organic farms do feed their soil and fight pests. They use natural methods, such as compost, manure, crop rotation, neem sprays and helpful insects, instead of factory-made chemicals.

sec.t:
The government set up training centres, gave farmers organic seeds and helped them build compost pits and vermicompost beds, where [[@earthworms|earthworms]] turn waste into rich fertiliser. Farmers learned to make sprays from neem, chillies and cow urine to keep insects away, and to plant different crops in turn so pests can't settle. Step by step, it reduced the chemicals it supplied. Then it banned their sale and use, with fines for breaking the rule.

About 75,000 hectares of farmland were certified organic. In 2018, Sikkim won the Future Policy Gold Award, given by the World Future Council together with the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization. It beat 51 other policies from around the world.

Sikkim is one of the world's biggest growers of large [[@cardamom-pepper|cardamom]], a smoky, dark spice used in curries and biryanis. Ginger, turmeric, buckwheat and Sikkim mandarin oranges also grow well there. Many of these now sell under an organic label for higher prices.

Not everything has gone smoothly. Some farmers say their harvests fell after the switch, and that they struggled with pests. Organic food is often more expensive, and Sikkim still brings in a lot of vegetables from neighbouring states, where chemicals are allowed. Researchers continue to study how well the policy works over time. Other Indian states, and countries such as [[@bhutan|Bhutan]], have watched closely, because Sikkim is one of the few places to have tried this across a whole region.

Sikkim was once an independent kingdom, ruled by kings called the Chogyals. In 1975, after a vote, it became India's 22nd state. Its people include Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali communities, and many follow Buddhism or Hinduism.

Kangchenjunga, the third-highest mountain in the world at about 8,586 m, rises on the border with Nepal. Many Sikkimese consider it a guardian deity. Out of respect, [[@mountaineering|climbers]] who reached its top from the Nepal side in 1955 deliberately stopped a few steps short of the very summit, and many climbers since have done the same.

text: Ink is a coloured liquid or paste made of two main things. The first is a colouring: tiny solid particles, called [[pigment|pigments]], or a dye that [[dissolve|dissolves]]. The second is a liquid to carry it, often with a binder, like gum or [[@glue-sticky|glue]], that helps it stick to the page.

The oldest inks were simple. Soot from lamps or fires was mixed with water and gum. Later people used plants, minerals, insects and metals. Indigo plants gave blue, and crushed lac insects gave red. Mixing new inks was a craft, and many scribes guarded their recipes. Today's inks are made in factories, with recipes for pens, printers, [[@newspapers|newspapers]] and even voting.

st.reveal: Silver nitrate soaks into the outer layer of skin and turns dark when light hits it. The mark only goes away as the skin cells naturally wear off, over days or weeks. It stops people voting twice.

sec.t:
For thousands of years, the most common ink was carbon black. Burn oil or wood with too little air, and you get fine black soot. Mix that soot with water and a binder, and you have ink that stays black for centuries. Egyptian scribes used it on papyrus about 4,500 years ago.

In China, makers mixed soot from burnt pine wood or oil with animal glue and pressed it into hard ink sticks. A writer ground the stick with water on a stone dish called an inkstone. Ink sticks are still used for [[@calligraphy|calligraphy]] and brush painting.

In India, scribes made an ink called masi from lampblack and other ingredients. Writers on palm leaves often scratched letters with a [[@writing-tools|stylus]] and rubbed soot into the lines afterwards.

sec.h: The ink that proves you voted
sec.t:
In India, every voter's left forefinger is marked with indelible ink, meaning ink that can't be removed. It contains silver nitrate, which reacts with the skin and darkens in light. The mark stays for days or weeks, which helps stop anyone [[@vote-how|voting]] twice.

Since 1962, this ink has been made by one company, Mysore Paints and Varnish Limited, in Mysuru, Karnataka. It is also sent to many other countries for their elections.

A ballpoint pen uses thick, oily ink that doesn't drip. A tiny ball at the tip rolls it onto the paper. Gel pens use a jelly-like ink with pigments. Felt-tip markers use runny ink that soaks along fibres.

Printers use different inks again. Newspaper presses use cheap, fast-drying oily inks in four colours: cyan, magenta, yellow and black. Together, these make almost any colour as tiny dots. The same four-colour idea is used in your home [[@printers|inkjet printer]].

Animals make ink too. Octopuses and [[@giant-squid|squid]] squirt a dark cloud of [[@octopus-ink|ink]] to confuse [[predator|predators]]. [[@power-cuttlefish|Cuttlefish ink]] was once used by artists, and its brown colour is called sepia. Many old photographs have a brownish sepia tone, though that colour comes from chemicals, not from cuttlefish.

text: A factory makes bread the same basic way a home baker does. Flour, water, [[yeast|yeast]] and salt are mixed into dough. The dough rests and rises, gets baked, then cools. The difference is size and speed. Machines mix dough by the tonne, ovens bake thousands of loaves an hour, and blades slice them before they are bagged.

A large plant can take flour in at one end and send sealed loaves out of the other in about three hours. Most of that time is the dough rising and the bread cooling, because yeast and hot bread can't be hurried much.

myth: Factory bread rises because it is full of chemicals instead of yeast.

Most factory bread is raised with ordinary baker's yeast. Factories do add small amounts of other ingredients, such as fats or flour improvers, to keep loaves soft and even, and these are listed on the packet.

sec.t:
Flour arrives by lorry and is blown through pipes into tall silos. Computers weigh out flour, water, yeast and salt for each batch. Then a powerful mixer beats the dough for a few minutes.

In 1961 scientists at a research centre in Chorleywood, England, found that very fast, hard mixing could do in minutes what a long, slow rise usually does. Their method, the Chorleywood bread process, made bread cheaper and quicker. Most sliced bread in Britain is still made this way, and many factories in India use similar fast methods.

Next a machine chops the dough into equal lumps, each weighed to the gram. Rollers shape them and drop them into tins on a moving belt. The tins travel slowly through a warm, damp cabinet called a prover for about an hour.

In there, the yeast gets to work. This is [[@fermentation|fermentation]]: the yeast eats sugars and breathes out [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. The gas is trapped by [[gluten|gluten]], the stretchy protein in wheat, so the dough swells like a balloon in a tin.

In 1928 the Chillicothe Baking Company in Missouri began selling bread sliced by a machine invented by Otto Rohwedder. People loved the convenience, and the phrase "the greatest thing since sliced bread" was born from it.

Modern slicers use rows of thin, fast blades that cut a loaf in one pass. A machine then slips each loaf into a bag and seals it. A printer adds the date, and a [[@barcodes|barcode]] tells the shop's till what it is.

Leavened white bread came to India with European traders, and the Portuguese in Goa are often credited with spreading the bakery loaf known as pav. In 1965 the government set up Modern Bread, a large state company that made packaged loaves common in Indian cities. Today many brands sell sliced bread across the country, and it often ends up in a Mumbai vada pav or a school sandwich.

Factories also have to keep bread from going mouldy. Clean rooms, sealed bags and careful cooling all help it last a few days. Some loaves also contain a little preservative, which is one of the ideas behind [[@food-preserve|food preserving]].
